title: Heritage Bookbinding Elements Transform in Contemporary Sculptures by Adelene Koh
description: After visiting the New York Art Book Fair in 2011, Adelene Koh was smitten with the world of bookbinding. Her professional training commenced in J
body:
After visiting the New York Art Book Fair in 2011, Adelene Koh was smitten with the world of bookbinding. Her professional training commenced in Japan, then led her to London, and she’s now based in Taiwan, where she runs a studio called dddots. This year, Koh was one of 30 finalists for the Loewe Foundation Craft Prize, which celebrates innovation across a wide range of artisanship.
As a bookmaker and conservator, Koh draws upon the technical precision and heritage of bookmaking to create unique sculptures using paper and thread. Her work “Endless” was included in the prize’s exhibition of shortlisted artists, consisting of a kind of ouroboros-like cylinder of meticulously folded paper and edges stitched with colorful fiber. “The result is an endless loop of a book’s spine and fore-edge bound together by the English endband sewing techniques from the 18th and 19th centuries,” says a statement.

Sewn endbands are not exactly invisible, but they’re usually tucked snugly inside the cover. The thread is also not necessarily colorful, as it may be selected to blend in with the pages or other parts of the binding. For Koh, this underappreciated element becomes the highlight through vibrant combinations and rhythmic patterns. “I’m interested in bringing hidden elements of books into focus,” Koh says. “I’m drawn to the overlooked, the sidelined, the parts that quietly support everything else.”
The winner of this year’s competition is Jongjin Park, and Colossal readers may also recognize the work of finalist Xanthe Somers. See more on Koh’s Instagram.

Weekly Newsletter
                Your remedy against toxic people, Trump’s war against the Smithsonian, and saying goodbye to two giants of the arts.   
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            How many days of your life have been ruined because of someone else's fragile ego? How many times have so-called "friends" shamelessly stolen your ideas? In this month's Art Problems column, Paddy Johnson tackles an uncomfortable question: Why are there so many toxic people in the art world? Read her tips on how to protect yourself from insecure peers and bad-faith actors. Hope it helps. Speaking of toxic people, President Trump has ordered the installation of content warning signs outside the Smithsonian National Museum of American History to alert the public against the institution's alleged leftist bias. "No other president has seen fit to vandalize taxpayer-funded museums with a billboard telling people not to go inside, while directing them to more politically 'palatable' — which is to say extreme right-wing — revisions of the historical record," writes Ed Simon in a must-read opinion piece below.In other stories, this week we said goodbye to two giants: assemblage artist Betye Saar, who died just four days before her 100th birthday, and performance artist Simone Forti, who passed away at 91. We mourn their death while celebrating the massive legacies they've left behind.  —Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief


	
		
			Madrid Museum Puts Picasso in Dialogue With “African Guernica”
		
	
	
		Spanning over 25-feet wide and 11-feet high, Pablo Picasso’s painting “Guernica” (1937) is as monumental in size as it is in cultural significance. Its startling depiction of state brutality against civilians has made it an emblem of post-war Spanish identity, and its cry against violence has resonated with besieged people worldwide — from Vietnam to Gaza — throughout the past nine decades. 
A new annual exhibition series at the Museo Reina Sofía in Madrid, which has served as the canonical work’s permanent home since 1992, places “Guernica” in dialogue with other artworks. The new program, titled History Doesn’t Repeat Itself, but It Does Rhyme, partly aims to revisit the universal political impulses behind the anti-war painting — but its first iteration also exposes race as an urgent issue for contemporary art institutions in Spain. | Agnish Ray

Instead, our journalism is funded by readers like you: individuals who fight for integrity and justice during increasingly unjust times.With your support (as little as $6.67/month!), you are joining a community of people who value and advocate for independent journalism and greater transparency in the arts. The perks aren’t bad either…We hope you’ll join us.
                        
                        
                            Learn more
                        
                    NewsA recent psychological study on so-called “cancel culture” and artistic impact found that its respondents reacted more punitively toward an artist accused of sexual assault (SA) compared to an artist accused of murder.Art Movements: Todd Caissie is named the new executive director of the Montclair Art Museum. Plus, curators are named for the Aichi Triennale and Biennale of Sydney in our weekly roundup of industry news.Trump has ordered federal officials to install content warning labels outside the Smithsonian National Museum of American History after his administration accused the institution of “anti-white” practices.Japan’s historic Kumamoto Castle is damaged after a 7.1-magnitude earthquake hits the country.The European Central Bank reveals 10 shortlisted design proposals for euro banknotes centered on either the theme of “European culture” or “rivers and birds” — and Leonardo da Vinci is in one of the designs.The German publishing giant Steidl Verlag is facing an uncertain future after coming close to bankruptcy.Trump spends $5 million in public funds on the regilding of two of the DC equestrian statues, “Arts of War” and “Arts of Peace.”Trump Administration
From Our Critics

	
		
			Why Did Rembrandt Die Poor?
		
	
	
		Rembrandt pioneered the saleable self, but unlike his rival, Gerard Van Honthorst, failed to reconcile his personal vision with the market. | Natasha Seaman
	
	
		Read More
	


	
		
			The Shakers Weren’t Minimalists
		
	
	
		An exhibition posits that the sect happened upon the ideals of modern design, overlooking the contradictions and vitality of its culture. | Isabella Segalovich
	
	
		Read More
	


	
		
			Widline Cadet’s Doubled Diaspora
		
	
	
		The Haitian-born photographer explores how various media, from dusty analog photo albums to cell phone videos, store and shape personal histories of migration. | Debra Brehmer

			Art Problems: Why Are There So Many Toxic People in the Art World?
		
	
	
		Every industry has toxic people, but desperation gives the art-world toxicity its particular flavor. The field is full of people making and supporting art, but the money available from collectors, grants and philanthropy combined can’t sustain most of them. We fight over the scraps.

Some of us handle scarcity better than others, but nobody is their best self. | Paddy Johnson

			A View From the Easel
		
	
	
		Shahryar Nashat sculpts along to the sounds of Kelis’s “Milkshake” and experiments with “a nautical glue the color of honey.”

			Required Reading
		
	
	
		Remembering Betye Saar on her 100th birthday, saving a women’s sculpture garden, Emily Wilson breaks the internet, climate scientists on OnlyFans, and more.

		We honor explorer of diasporic consciousness, a revolutionary assemblage artist, and the first Black dean of art in the US.

title: Citing Censorship, Artist Emma Shapiro Launches Legal Challenge to Restore Instagram Account
description: On December 8, 2025, Instagram permanently terminated the account @nipeople, a project by artist, journalist, and activist Emma Shapiro, instantly e
body:
On December 8, 2025, Instagram permanently terminated the account @nipeople, a project by artist, journalist, and activist Emma Shapiro, instantly erasing years of work and sparking a legal debate over digital freedom.

	The Instagram account was part of Exposure Therapy, a project begun in 2017 that aims to challenge gender-based discrimination by highlighting the ways society’s sexualization of female-presenting bodies is reflected in various laws. Image after image of female nipples filled the feed, each posing the same question: Is any body inherently pornographic? 
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	The conversation was cut short in 2025, when Meta, the parent company of Instagram, suspended the account after Shapiro posted a short video depicting a utility pole plastered in Exposure Therapy’s nipple stickers, pointing to alleged violations of its “account integrity” policies.

	@nipeople was deleted one day later, after Shapiro submitted an appeal through Instagram’s in-app review process. Shapiro, who was born in the US but lives in Spain, has since taken legal action with the aid of Avant-Garde Lawyers (AGL), a group specializing in cases involving creative censorship. In June, AGL filed a complaint with the Spanish Comisión Nacional de los Mercados y la Competencia (CNMC) on behalf of the artist, arguing that Meta failed to comply with several obligations under the European Union’s Digital Services Act (DSA).

	“Meta failed to provide a sufficiently clear statement of reasons for its decision, denied Shapiro access to an effective internal complaint-handling process, and failed to act in a diligent, objective and proportionate manner when imposing the severe sanction of permanent account termination,” AGL said in a statement. 


			
			
			
	
			
					A screenshot of Meta notifying Emma Shapiro that the appeal to restore the @nipeople account was denied.
									Courtesy the artist
	



	There are two separate procedures for the complaint: one is an out-of-court dispute resolution procedure through User Rights, a European settlement body serving content moderation issues, which, as confirmed by the Art Newspaper, has contacted Meta for details of the case. The second is a complaint to the CNMC, Spain’s Digital Services Coordinator, which has yet to begin its formal assessment 
	

	“This case is personal, but the issue is systemic,” Shapiro told ARTnews via email. “Artists and other users are increasingly subject to opaque decisions by digital platforms that can erase years of work without adequate explanation or an effective avenue for appeal.” 

	Shapiro added that she has seen these challenges firsthand through her work as editor-at-large of Don’t Delete Art, a collaborative project of the National Coalition Against Censorship’s Arts and Culture Advocacy program, which advocates for artistic freedom online. The site tracks incidents of alleged artistic censorship, joining a growing number of digital archives and reporting tools that have emerged in recent years to document threats to creative expression and First Amendment rights.

	In her email, Shapiro continued, “For artists, the greatest danger isn’t just that a work is removed. It’s that the fear of arbitrary removal changes what gets created in the first place. When people cannot trust that their work will be treated fairly, many stop experimenting, avoid controversial subjects, or censor themselves before anyone else does. That chilling effect is one of the most serious consequences of unaccountable platform power.”

	Andra Matei, AGL’s Executive Director and legal lead on the case, said in a statement that, “For an artist, losing an account can mean losing years of work, audience, income and visibility overnight,” adding that “The DSA is meant to ensure that platforms are not beyond legal scrutiny. Meta is powerful, but it is not outside the law”.

body:
July 31, 2026 5:16pm	
					
							
		
			
				

			
	
			
	


				

	Summer reading enters its final stretch as 6 exciting new books hit the shelves in August (if you don’t count my own!). 

	This month’s offerings span the centuries, moving from Renaissance theories of vision to contemporary debates over morality, inequality, and the future of art.

	A new biography explores the secret lives of John Singer Sargent, the queer Gilded Age society painter whose dazzling surfaces concealed a more guarded inner world. A manifesto by the artist collective Metahaven asks about the changing role of art as AI wreaks havoc on our attention span and climate change dampens our capacity to imagine a future. Journalist Hettie Judah guides readers through the opaque creature that is the art world, offering practical advice while puncturing a few of its more stubborn myths. Meanwhile, Daisy Dixon’s Depraved: The Story of Dangerous Art blends history and philosophy to explore a subject as timely as it is timeless, tracing anxieties around obscenity, taste, and public offense back to prehistoric art. 

	Whether you’re working in your last beach reads, looking for smart company on a long plane ride, or studying up for a September syllabus, we’ve got the latest and greatest listed for you below.

	Happy reading!


			
			
	Depraved: The Story of Dangerous Art
			
								
				

	By Daisy Dixon

	Philosopher Daisy Dixon asks what moral and aesthetic sentiments we are expressing when we—or they—refer to an artwork as “depraved.” Taking us across time and genre—from prehistoric Venus figurines to Cardi B and Megan Thee Stallion’s WAP—she weaves, too, between historical examples and philosophical musings. This range-y lookback has a pointed resonance with the here and now—that is, MAGA’s ongoing assault on culture.

		
			
			
	The Photographic World Picture: A New Prehistory of Photography
			
								
				

	By Andrew Moisey

	Depending on who you ask—and what counts as a photograph—2026 marks 200 years since the technology’s invention. But of course, in the runup to the world’s first photo came a lot of exploring. Cornell art historian Andrew Moisey looks all the way back to the Renaissance, arguing that proto-photographic ideas of instantaneity first appeared in painting before showing how photography indelibly altered the canvases of modernists.

		
			
			
	The Hard Question of Art: Cognitive Futures
			
								
				

	By Metahaven

	Challenging times prompt existential questions, and here, Metahaven takes a stab at answering them. Looking to how climate change, AI, and rampant inequality have assaulted our attention spans and reoriented our ability to imagine a future, the artist collective asks what all this means for art—reliant as it is on both attention and imagination.

		
			
			
	Beyond Beauty: A Portrait of John Singer Sargent
			
								
				

	By Devon Cox

	The indelible chronicler of Gilded Age glamor, who made so many portraits of society’s finest, here gets a portrait of his own. Biographer Devon Cox tackles the queer artist’s “guarded inner life,” promising readers a character who is “restless, deceptively daring, and shrouded in secrecy.” He argues, too, that Sargent left clues to the inner lives of the socialites he painted.

		
			
			
	How to Enter the Art World
			
								
				

	By Hettie Judah

	Targeted toward artists, this book, by journalist Hettie Judah, offers pointers toward navigating the art world, demystifying its unspoken rules and debunking its myths. Based on years of conversations with artists and arts professionals, it dispels the notion that an artist’s career is ever linear.

		
			
			
	Still Dangerous!: The Harmony Hammond Reader
			
								
				

	By Harmony Hammond

	Lately, Harmony Hammond figured in the 2024 Whitney Biennial and mounted a survey at SITE Santa Fe. But long before that, she co-founded the storied feminist collective A.I.R. Gallery and wrote tirelessly (for this magazine and others) on the work of women and lesbian artists, fighting their structural exclusion from the art world. A new collection of her writings, edited by Tirza True Latimer with a foreword by Julia Bryan-Wilson, is a portrait of her perseverance.

schema.headline: 6 Books We’re Looking Forward to in August
